title: Modernising payment services regulation: consultation
date_evidence: This consultation ran from 3pm on 14 July 2026 to 11:59pm on 6 October 2026 (gov.uk consultation page); PDF cover: July 2026
key_claim: The consultation asks in Question 15 whether authentication, consent and liability for unauthorised payment transactions need updating for agentic payments, concedes the PSRs may not fully facilitate agentic AI, closed on 6 October 2026, and gives no date for the wider reforms beyond a promise of further detail after the consultation.
frame_summary: The Treasury frames agentic payments as an opportunity to lead and puts liability to the market as an open question rather than proposing a rule.
verbatim_quote: However, the PSRs were designed before the development of AI and may not fully facilitate the use of agentic AI.
verbatim_list: The Government wants the UK to be at the forefront of the global development of agentic payments
authentication and consent of payments transactions, and liability for unauthorised payment transactions, need updating
The Government will set out further detail about how these reforms will be implemented following the consultation.
lay a statutory instrument under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 by the end of 2026
notes: Structural anchor (97 days before scan date). Publication date 14 July 2026 read from the gov.uk consultation page via WebFetch 19/10/2026; the PDF cover carries July 2026 and the paragraph and page references (3.32, 3.35, Question 15 on p. 22, 5.1 on p. 40, 1.6 and 1.11) come from the PDF. title: Call for expressions of interest in a new wave of digital euro innovation platform activities
date_evidence: 28 September 2026 (date on the title page of the call document)
key_claim: The ECB's call covers AI-enabled payment experiences and AI agents but places cybersecurity, fraud prevention, compliance and risk management outside its scope; applications close on 9 November 2026 and experimentation runs from January to June 2027.
frame_summary: The ECB presents agent payments as a design-exploration topic for the digital euro and carves out fraud, compliance and risk from that work.
verbatim_quote: AI-enabled payment experiences, AI agents, micropayments and machine-to-machine interactions
verbatim_list: Topics related to cybersecurity, fraud prevention, compliance, risk management
notes: Fetched via WebFetch 19/10/2026. Experimentation dates (January to June 2027) read from the same document; the exclusion sentence was extracted verbatim up to the words risk management.

title: Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI): Final report
date_evidence: 15 October 2026 (date line of the FSB final report page)
key_claim: The final report sets out 12 sound practices, including that financial institutions define clear roles and responsibilities and implement appropriate and effective human oversight; it frames them for institutions' own AI governance.
frame_summary: The FSB argues that responsible AI adoption is a matter of each institution's governance, accountability and human oversight rather than of allocating customer losses.
verbatim_quote: Financial institutions define clear roles and responsibilities
verbatim_list: Financial institutions implement appropriate and effective human oversight
This report sets out 12 sound practices
notes: Fetched via WebFetch 19/10/2026. The extraction showed no mention of payments on the page; the reading that the practices address institutional governance rather than customer loss allocation is the analyst's.

title: Agentic payments liability: what UK payment law answers, and what it does not
date_evidence: Published 22 July 2026 (last updated 18 August 2026), Rob Bratby (byline)
key_claim: The Payment Services Regulations 2017 largely govern agent-initiated payments between payer and provider; what they do not settle is the scope of a delegation exercised by software, and neither the refund regime nor the push-payment reimbursement regime allocates loss to the party that supplied the agent.
frame_summary: A payments lawyer argues the existing rules still answer most agent-payment cases and that the open question is how far a software agent's delegation extends.
verbatim_quote: What the regulations do not settle is the scope of a delegation exercised by software.
verbatim_list: Whether the payer consented under regulation 67 determines whether the provider must refund under regulation 76
That is an open question rather than a finding that the current rules have ceased to apply.
notes: Fetched via WebFetch 19/10/2026. The statements about the push-payment reimbursement regime and about the supplier of the agent are faithful summaries of the article, not quotes.

title: Opinion: Who pays when an AI agent exceeds its authority
date_evidence: October 9, 2026 (Opinion section byline date), Aaron Cheiffetz
key_claim: There is no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate; Regulation E and Regulation Z turn on whether a transaction was authorised, and Visa and Mastercard zero-liability policies do not clearly resolve a consumer-authorised agent's out-of-scope purchase.
frame_summary: An opinion piece argues that US consumer-payment rules hinge on authorisation and so leave agent out-of-scope losses unallocated.
verbatim_quote: There's no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate
verbatim_list: They don't clearly resolve what happens when a consumer authorized an agent to transact
notes: Opinion column by an adviser to banks, used as corroboration for the US position. Apostrophes on the page may be typographic; quote confirmed by WebFetch extraction 19/10/2026.

title: Agentic commerce liability is still being written
date_evidence: Published July 30, 2026 (modified August 11, 2026), Reshmi Suresh, Head of Agentic Commerce
key_claim: Clear fraud cases follow existing authenticated tokenised-transaction rules, but no liability shift exists yet and disputes short of outright fraud, such as an agent misreading an instruction, have no clean answer; issuers tend to side with the cardholder.
frame_summary: An acquirer argues that card-network rules cover agent fraud but leave non-fraud agent disputes unallocated, pushing merchants to keep their own intent records.
verbatim_list: liability generally follows existing authenticated tokenized-transaction rules
issuers tend to side with the cardholder
Where it gets murkier is everything short of outright fraud.
notes: Vendor source (acquirer), used as directional corroboration of card-network practice; fetched via WebFetch 19/10/2026.
